newsitem.title: UK: NYMEX says "closely monitoring" heating oil market.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX says "closely monitoring" heating oil market.

text.p: The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) is "closely monitoring" its heating oil futures market heading into winter due to recent volatility, after a sharp rally lifted prices to their highest level since the Gulf War, NYMEX Chairman Daniel Rappaport said on Tuesday.

But he said no problems were expected in deliveries against the contract in New York Harbor, the heart of the northeast U.S. which is the largest heating oil market in the world, and no extra precautions on margins or price limits were being taken.
Rappaport said prices could rise more since distillate inventories were now at levels similar to before the cold snap of December 1989 when prices rose to $1.10 a gallon.

"We are closely monitoring it. We are always concerned when stocks are at low levels. However, I don't see any real problems," he told Reuters after a press conference as part of his visit for activities at London Metal Exchange Week.
"Clearly, when there is more volatility we monitor it more closely," he said, adding that the exchange already reviews margins on a daily basis.
The spot month contract is now trading at about 76 cents and has jumped about 38 percent in value since late July.
"I wouldn't be surprised for prices to go higher (if) only because the inventory level is at the point now when prices were above $1 (in December 1989)," he said.

Total U.S. distillate stocks, according to the American Petroleum Institute, stand at 112.3 million barrels and high sulphur heating oil inventories in the Northeast are 23.7 million, off 18.7 and 18.6 million from a year ago respectively.

In early October 1989, total U.S. distillate stocks were 121.8 million and total distillates in the Northeast were 49.0 million, API said. API did not break down distillates into low and high sulphur at that time.

Separately, Rappaport said its dormant sour crude contract was dealt a "big blow" when the United Nations imposed trade sanctions on Iraq shortly after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990. Iraq's production of 3.14 million barrels a day at the time was all sour crude.
"We still look at the sour crude contract as perhaps a possibility for the Asian benchmark...We consider and always consider sour crude contract with a Gulf Coast delivery as a possibility," he said.
